channel.title: Investigating Chronos-2
channel.description: A measured study of a time-series foundation model on the M5 benchmark: a gradient-boosted baseline, the foundation model, and what it takes to find out whether the remaining headroom is reachable.

item.title: Difficulty belongs to the item, and mostly to its volume
item.description:
The previous post ended flat: covariates lost, cross-learning lost, a 46-length context sweep bought 0.11%, a LoRA fine-tune was a wash. One lever was left — treat different items differently: fine-tune per group, cross-learn inside a group, one model per group.

That lever has a precondition, and the precondition is testable before any of it is built. For a static grouping to help, difficulty has to be a stable property of an item. If the items that are hard this week are not the ones that were hard last week, no grouping — hand-made, clustered or learned — has anything to hold on to.

This post answers that, and then keeps narrowing. Difficulty is a stable property of the item. Two thirds of it is volume, which needs no clustering to exploit. The third that survives is real — bigger than every other term in the budget except the irreducible noise — and it is not in the weekly shape, which is the one candidate axis this study had built the apparatus to test.

Three answers, and the last one is the kind of negative result worth publishing: bounded, and it redirects the work rather than ending it.

The panel

Twenty-four origins, one week apart, scored over 7-day non-overlapping windows. Non-overlapping matters: with overlapping windows the correlation between consecutive origins would be partly an artefact of shared days. The model is the zero-shot one at the context length chosen for days 1–7 — the fine-tuned model is disqualified here, because walking its test-origin checkpoint backwards would let it see the future of every earlier window.

The origins run 2015-10-18 to 2016-03-27. Of the 494 series scorable at least once, 138 are scorable at every origin, and those are the panel. That count is printed rather than buried: double-centring a grid with holes is a different estimator, and a series present at half the origins would have its difficulty measured on a different set of weeks than its neighbours’.

Show the code 
order = np.argsort(result.alpha)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.5))
image = ax.imshow(panel.x[order], aspect="auto", cmap="RdYlBu_r", interpolation="nearest",
                  vmin=np.quantile(panel.x, 0.02), vmax=np.quantile(panel.x, 0.98))
ax.set_xlabel("origin (one week apart, oldest left)")
ax.set_ylabel("item, sorted by average difficulty")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, n_origins, 4))
ax.set_xticklabels([str(panel.origins[i]) for i in range(0, n_origins, 4)],
                   rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="log WQL", shrink=0.85)
plt.show()

The error of each (item, origin) cell splits four ways:

is the item — by construction the only part a static grouping could exploit. is the week: some weeks are hard for everyone. What is left splits further into a part that survives to the next origin, a part that does not, and the sampling noise of the cell itself, measured from the odd and even days of each window.

Does the estimator work?

This is the step most analyses skip, and the one that decides whether anything here means anything. Before the real panel, a simulated one with known components, at this panel’s size and noise level:

Show the code 
control, planted = simulate_panel(n_series=250, n_origins=N_ORIGINS, seed=SEED)
recovered = decompose(control).shares()
components = ["series", "origin", "persistent", "transient", "noise"]
md(pl.DataFrame({
    "component": components,
    "planted %": [100 * planted[c] for c in components],
    "recovered %": [100 * recovered["series_adjusted" if c == "series" else c]
                    for c in components],
}), digits=1)

Two further controls run silently and both pass: a panel with no item effect returns 0.8% after bias adjustment rather than the 4.5% the raw estimator reports, and a pure-noise panel returns a persistence of +0.005 rather than the negative value double-centring would otherwise induce.

The control also exposes the method’s one real limit. A difficulty that drifts slowly is partly indistinguishable from a constant one over a panel spanning six months, so it gets shared between the item term and the persistent term. Sweeping the drift’s autocorrelation from 0 to 0.97 moves the split between those two from 0.7%/0% to 15.9%/2.0% — while their sum stays put. So two readings get reported: the item share answers could a grouping fitted once and left alone help, and the sum answers is there anything stable at all, even if it has to be refitted.

Where the error lives

Show the code 
intervals = bootstrap_shares(panel, n_draws=1000, seed=SEED)
md(pl.DataFrame([
    {"component": name, "share %": 100 * shares[key],
     "CI low %": 100 * intervals[key][0], "CI high %": 100 * intervals[key][1]}
    for name, key in [("item (raw)", "series"),
                      ("item (bias-adjusted)", "series_adjusted"),
                      ("week", "origin"),
                      ("item x week", "interaction"),
                      ("  - persistent", "persistent"),
                      ("  - transient", "transient"),
                      ("  - sampling noise", "noise"),
                      ("stable (item + persistent)", "stable")]]), digits=1)

Two numbers carry the section. The identity of the item accounts for 42% of the variance in log WQL once the noise inside each is removed. And the week accounts for 2% — there are essentially no weeks that are hard for everybody. Difficulty has an address, and the address is the item.

Most of what remains is sampling noise, which is what forecasting 7-day windows of items selling a few units a week buys you. That matters for the next section rather than being an aside.

Two instruments, one answer

A decomposition is a model, and a model can be wrong. Rank agreement is not a model: order the items by error at one origin, order them again at the next, and ask whether the two orderings agree.

Show the code 
ranks = rank_agreement(panel, decile=0.10)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax = axes[0]
values = ranks["consecutive"]
ax.plot(range(1, len(values) + 1), values, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, marker="o", markersize=4)
ax.axhline(ranks["consecutive_median"], color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.axhspan(-0.5, 0.5, color=plots.GRID_COLOR, alpha=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.text(0.98, 0.04, "|rho| < 0.5: 'weak' for test-retest", transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha="right", va="bottom", color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(-1, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("pair of consecutive origins")
ax.set_ylabel("Spearman of the difficulty ranking")
ax = axes[1]
first, last = panel.x[:, 0], panel.x[:, -1]
ax.scatter(first, last, s=10, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, alpha=0.6)
limits = [min(first.min(), last.min()), max(first.max(), last.max())]
ax.plot(limits, limits, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel(f"log WQL at {panel.origins[0]}")
ax.set_ylabel(f"... at {panel.origins[-1]}")
ax.text(0.03, 0.95, f"Spearman {ranks['first_vs_last']:+.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
        va="top", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

A median of +0.52 between consecutive origins looks like weak agreement. Test–retest conventions call anything under 0.5 weak, and the pre-registered rule for this study wanted 0.6. Taken at face value, the two sections of this post seem to disagree: a large item effect, and a ranking that only half holds.

They do not disagree. The decomposition predicts the rank correlation, and the prediction can be written down from the variance shares alone.

Within one origin the week effect is a constant and does not touch the across-items ranking, so the spread of the measured error at a single origin is , while the covariance between two consecutive origins keeps only the parts that survive the step, . Their ratio is the correlation the model expects anyone to observe. Six months apart the persistent part has decayed and only remains.

Divide instead by the reliable part of a cell — everything except the sampling noise — and you get the correlation between the underlying difficulties rather than between their noisy estimates.

Show the code 
v_alpha = shares["series_adjusted"]
v_pers, v_trans, v_noise = shares["persistent"], shares["transient"], shares["noise"]
cell_variance = v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans + v_noise
reliability = (v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans) / cell_variance

attenuation = pl.DataFrame([
    {"quantity": "consecutive origins",
     "predicted": (v_alpha + v_pers) / cell_variance,
     "observed": ranks["consecutive_median"],
     "noise-corrected": (v_alpha + v_pers) / (v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans)},
    {"quantity": "first vs last origin",
     "predicted": v_alpha / cell_variance,
     "observed": ranks["first_vs_last"],
     "noise-corrected": v_alpha / (v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans)},
])
md(attenuation, digits=3)

A single 7-day window is only 56% reliable: more than two fifths of its variance is the counting noise of an item that sells a handful of units a week. Seen through a ruler that blunt, a difficulty ordering stable at 0.86 between consecutive origins can only show up as +0.52 — which is what it did, to within a few hundredths of the predicted value, on both rows, with the two residuals falling on opposite sides. That is what sampling variation looks like; a systematic error in the variance model would push both the same way.

So the observed +0.52 was never evidence of weak stability. It was evidence of a noisy ruler, and the agreement between the predicted and observed columns is the strongest internal check in this post: a variance model and a distribution-free rank statistic, built on different assumptions, returning the same number.

The six-month row says something further. Nearly all of the long-run agreement is the term — the persistent part has decayed by then — so is behaving like a genuinely fixed property of the item rather than a slow drift.

The pre-registered rule, and what to do with it

Partial persistence: weigh the gain against the complexity.
  series (bias-adjusted) 41.7% of the variance, median consecutive-origin Spearman +0.52, first vs last +0.41
  stable at all (series + persistent) 45.7%, of which persistent 4.0%

The rule, fixed before any of this was computed: a median consecutive-origin Spearman of 0.6 or more and at least 35% of the variance on the item means a grouping has something real; 0.3 or less, or under 20%, means it has not; between the two, partial. It returns partial, on one arm only — the variance share clears its bar comfortably, the Spearman does not.

Moving a pre-registered threshold after seeing the data is exactly the move this study is built to avoid, so the rule stays as written and its verdict stays reported. But the rule was mis-specified, and identifiably so before any data arrived: its Spearman arm bounds a quantity that the sampling noise of a 7-day window attenuates, and the thresholds were taken from published work on windows of a different reliability. The honest record is both numbers — the rule as written returns partial, and the quantity the rule was reaching for is 0.86.

On the question the rule was asked to settle, the evidence is one-directional:

  • the item carries 42% of the variance, CI [36, 48];
  • the week carries 2%;
  • the underlying difficulty ordering holds at 0.86 week to week and 0.78 across six months;
  • and both known biases of the method push toward a large item effect, so 42% is better read as an upper bound than as a point estimate.

Difficulty is a stable property of the item. The precondition holds.

Most of it is volume

A large item share is the start of an argument, not the end of one. WQL is scale-free, so a dependence on volume would not be an artefact of units — it would be a statement about predictability: an item selling a third of a unit a day has an irreducibly high relative error, and that is a permanent property of the item.

That distinction decides what is worth. If it is a function of volume, then “group the items by difficulty” means “bucket them by volume”, which needs no clustering and which the forecaster reads off the history unaided.

One correction is mandatory and easy to miss. The sampling noise of a 7-day window is itself strongly volume-dependent, so low-volume items have their inflated more — which would manufacture exactly the relationship being tested for. A global bias adjustment cannot fix a bias that differs per item, so each item’s noise is measured from its own odd and even days and removed individually.

Show the code 
volume_record = RECORD["stable_vs_volume"]
rho = volume_record["spearman"]
md(pl.DataFrame([
    {"removed": "nothing (raw item effect)", "Spearman with alpha": None,
     "item share of the budget %": 100 * volume_record["share_raw"]},
    {"removed": "each item's own measured noise", "Spearman with alpha": None,
     "item share of the budget %": 100 * volume_record["share_noise_corrected"]},
    {"removed": "+ log volume", "Spearman with alpha": rho["log volume"],
     "item share of the budget %": None},
    {"removed": "+ zero-day share", "Spearman with alpha": rho["zero-day share"],
     "item share of the budget %": None},
    {"removed": "+ both covariates", "Spearman with alpha": None,
     "item share of the budget %": 100 * volume_record["share_after_covariates"]},
]), digits=2)
Show the code 
prior = SALES.filter(pl.col("date") <= ORIGINS[0], ~pl.col("is_missing"))
profile = (prior.group_by("id")
           .agg(pl.col("sales").mean().alias("mean_daily"),
                (pl.col("sales") == 0).mean().alias("zero_share")))
aligned = pl.DataFrame({"id": panel.ids}).join(profile, on="id", how="left")
log_volume = np.log(np.maximum(aligned["mean_daily"].to_numpy(), 1e-3))

from m5_chronos2.persistence import series_noise
precision = 1 / np.maximum(series_noise(panel), np.percentile(series_noise(panel), 5))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
for ax, x, label in [(axes[0], log_volume, "log mean units sold per day"),
                     (axes[1], aligned["zero_share"].to_numpy(), "share of zero-sale days")]:
    ax.scatter(x, result.alpha, s=6 + 40 * precision / precision.max(),
               color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, alpha=0.55, edgecolor="none")
    ax.set_xlabel(label)
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\alpha_i$  (stable difficulty)")
axes[0].text(0.03, 0.06, f"Spearman {rho['log volume']:+.2f}", transform=axes[0].transAxes,
             color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
axes[1].text(0.03, 0.94, f"Spearman {rho['zero-day share']:+.2f}",
             transform=axes[1].transAxes, va="top", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Volume and sparsity together explain 63% of the stable difficulty. Two details matter for reading that.

They are not two explanations. Volume alone reaches the same 63%; adding the zero-day share moves nothing. At a Spearman of +0.71 with and a near-mechanical relationship to volume on data that is two thirds zeros, sparsity is a second view of the same quantity, not an independent factor.

And the noise channel is not what is driving it. A variance subtraction fixes an inflated spread, not an inflated level, and is a log, so a noisier estimate of the same underlying error need not have the same expectation. The direct test is to ask how much of the measurement noise itself explains: it reaches 0.63 as a Spearman against 0.77 for volume, and 34% of the variance against 63%. If the volume relationship were an artefact of the noise level, the noise level would be the proximate cause and the stronger correlate. It is the weaker one, by a clear margin.

So two thirds of the stable item effect is a sort on a number already in the history, and one third is not: 15.6% of the whole error budget, against 2.0% for the week and 11.5% for everything transient. It is the largest addressable term left, and the only one a grouping could earn its keep on.

Is the rest of it in the weekly shape?

The residual is real. The question is where to look for it, and this study had already built the machinery to look in one specific place: the weekly shape — the share of a week falling on each weekday. Each week is normalised to 1, the weeks are pooled, and the result is a 7-vector summing to 1, so how much an item sells drops out and only when it sells remains.

Show the code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.3]})
ax = axes[0]
generator = np.random.default_rng(0)
for index in generator.choice(len(X), size=min(40, len(X)), replace=False):
    ax.plot(range(WEEKDAYS), X[index], color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, alpha=0.18, linewidth=1)
ax.plot(range(WEEKDAYS), X.mean(axis=0), color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=2.5)
ax.axhline(1 / WEEKDAYS, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
ax.text(0.02, 1 / WEEKDAYS, " a flat week", va="bottom", ha="left",
        color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xticks(range(WEEKDAYS)); ax.set_xticklabels(DAY_NAMES)
ax.set_ylabel("share of the week")
ax = axes[1]
weekend = X[:, 5] + X[:, 6]
image = ax.imshow(X[np.argsort(weekend)], aspect="auto", cmap="RdYlBu_r",
                  interpolation="nearest", vmin=np.quantile(X, 0.02),
                  vmax=np.quantile(X, 0.98))
ax.set_xticks(range(WEEKDAYS)); ax.set_xticklabels(DAY_NAMES)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("item, sorted by weekend share")
ax.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="share of the week", shrink=0.9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Here is that construction, animated, on planted archetypes: four invented weekly shapes, scattered and then redrawn as counts at the items’ real weekly totals. It is synthetic data, and saying so is the point — it shows what the space is and what genuine structure in it would look like, which is what makes the measurement below legible either way.

Shape is worth testing because it is a different axis from volume by construction. But that is also why the link cannot be assumed: the dominant component of the item effect has been removed from the object on purpose, so whether anything of the item effect is left in that object is an open empirical question — and the cheapest one available, because it decides whether a clustering of the shape space is worth building at all.

The test regresses on volume, sparsity and the per-item noise level, then adds the six free shape coordinates and asks what they add. Three things make it readable:

  • Shape is measured on history strictly before the panel’s first origin. A profile computed over the scored windows would be partly measured on what it predicts.
  • Six extra regressors explain variance by construction — about of what is left. That is removed in expectation, and a permutation test gives the distribution instead of the expectation. The shuffle is stratified by volume, so the null keeps whatever relationship shape has with volume and destroys only its link to difficulty. Permuting freely would break the shape–volume relationship too, make the null easier to beat, and bias the test toward finding an effect.
  • Shape is itself measured with error, and error in a predictor attenuates what it explains toward zero — the mirror image of the attenuation above. So the increment is reported both as measured and divided by the shape’s own reliability, as an upper bound on what a perfectly measured shape could contribute.
Show the code 
bridge = RECORD["shape_vs_alpha"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.15]})

ax = axes[0]
bars = [("observed", bridge["increment"], plots.MAIN_COLOR),
        ("null median", bridge["null_median"], plots.GRID_COLOR),
        ("null 95th pct", bridge["null_p95"], plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR),
        ("ceiling if shape\nwere perfect", bridge["increment_disattenuated"],
         plots.TEXT_COLOR)]
ax.barh([b[0] for b in bars], [100 * b[1] for b in bars],
        color=[b[2] for b in bars], height=0.6)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("share of the stable difficulty that shape explains (%)")
ax.text(0.97, 0.08, f"p = {bridge['p_value']:.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha="right", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)

ax = axes[1]
ax.bar(range(WEEKDAYS), bridge["spearman_per_weekday"], color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, width=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(WEEKDAYS)); ax.set_xticklabels(DAY_NAMES)
ax.set_ylim(-0.4, 0.4)
ax.set_ylabel(r"Spearman with $\alpha_i$")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The weekly shape carries essentially none of it. The observed increment is 0.7% of the stable difficulty, below the null’s 95th percentile of 1.5%, at p = 0.15 over 1000 permutations in 10 volume strata. Shape explains less than a typical volume-preserving shuffle does.

And the result is bounded, not merely absent. The profile’s own split-half reliability on these items is 0.44, so a perfectly measured weekly shape could account for at most 1.5% — the fourth bar above. There is no version of this measurement, however much the ruler improves, in which the weekly shape reaches the 15.6% that is still on the item.

Three details that keep it from being an artefact of the setup. 135 of 138 panel items have a 26-week shape before the first origin, so the sub-population is the panel; reliability here (0.44) is better than across the full roster, because the panel’s members are the steady sellers, so this is the favourable corner of the data for shape; and the per-weekday correlations on the right never leave ±0.16, so no single weekday carries difficulty either.

And the audit that was already running

By the time that test existed, the shape space had already been put through a full clustering audit: does the population contain discrete types, or is it one continuum? That audit is worth reporting, with its result stated plainly and its standing corrected.

Show the code 
strengths = {int(k): v for k, v in AUDIT["prediction_strength"].items()}
md(pl.DataFrame([
    {"quantity": "items audited", "value": float(AUDIT["n_series_audited"])},
    {"quantity": "profile reliability (bar is 0.80)", "value": AUDIT["split_half_audited"]},
    {"quantity": "reproducible cluster count K-hat", "value": float(AUDIT["k_hat"])},
    {"quantity": f"best prediction strength (at K={max(strengths, key=strengths.get)})",
     "value": max(strengths.values())},
    {"quantity": "separation achieved", "value": AUDIT["separation_achieved"]},
    {"quantity": "detection floor from the positive control",
     "value": AUDIT["detection_floor_delta"]},
    {"quantity": "null's worst spread ratio (refuse above 1.5)",
     "value": AUDIT["null_geometry_worst_spread_ratio"]},
    {"quantity": "calendar-alignment lift over random rotation",
     "value": AUDIT["alignment"]["lift"]},
]), digits=3)
Inconclusive: the fitted null does not reproduce the real cloud's geometry, so its p-value cannot be read.

Two of its four conditions could not be evaluated, and they fail in opposite directions.

The population was never filtered. The audit was written to keep only the volume deciles whose profile clears a 0.80 reliability bar. No decile cleared it — reliability runs from 0.21 in the sparsest tenth to 0.70 in the densest — so nothing was filtered and the audit ran on all 493 items, including the half whose week-to-week shape variation is indistinguishable from multinomial counting noise. Clustering a cloud in which half the points are near-random draws around the population mean pushes the estimated cluster count toward one, which is the result obtained. The negative finding is the one that defect compromises.

And the null is not usable. It is fitted to the real cloud — dominant axis by SVD, a smooth manifold along it, Gaussian residuals carrying the real residual covariance — but its worst per-coordinate spread comes out 3.9× the real cloud’s, against a refusal threshold of 1.5. A null more diffuse than the data clusters less reproducibly, so the real data beats it too easily and the p-value is biased toward finding structure. So p = 0.024 — which equals its own floor with 40 nulls — cannot be read either.

It would have been easy to publish a continuum here. on the real data, every one of the 40 nulls also returning 1, separation 0.00 against a detection floor of 1.50 — three true sentences from which “one continuum, no discrete types” follows smoothly. The checks standing in the way are checks this analysis imposed on itself, and they say the smooth conclusion is unsupported in both directions.

One part of the audit does pass cleanly, and it is a positive structural result: the weekly shapes are anchored to the calendar. The rotation that best aligns a pair of profiles is zero for 37% of pairs against 14% for a randomly rotated copy — a lift of ×2.58. Euclidean distance on these 7-vectors is measuring shape, not clock offset.

What the bridge test does to all of this. Repairing the null and restoring the power were the obvious next steps, and they are no longer worth taking for this purpose: shape carries at most 1.5% of the difficulty that volume leaves unexplained, so even a repaired audit returning crisp discrete types would be organising almost none of the error.

That is not the same as the work being wasted. The audit answers a real question about the data — do items form types in weekly shape — now known to be decoupled from forecast difficulty. And there is a symmetry worth noticing: the audit found shape strongly volume-dependent in its measurability, and the bridge test found it nearly independent of difficulty in its content. Both say the same thing from opposite ends. Shape and difficulty are different axes, and the chain that ran from one to the other was assumed rather than measured.

Where this leaves the question

Established. 42% of the variance in log WQL sits on the identity of the item against 2% on the week, with an underlying week-to-week stability of 0.86 and a six-month stability of 0.78. Of that, 63% is volume — a continuous covariate already present in the history, needing no clustering. The 15.6% that remains is item-specific, stable, and not in the weekly shape, at a ceiling of 1.5%. The shape space is calendar-anchored, and its measurability rises monotonically with volume.

Open. Whether that residual is organised at all, and on what axis. Candidates this study has not tested: burstiness and volatility, lifecycle stage, promotion and price response, intermittency structure beyond the zero-day share. Each is one covariate block through the same machinery — the test is cheap now that the panel and the estimator exist, and a negative is as useful as a positive because it is bounded.

And two limits that no further run removes. The bridge test is linear in the shape coordinates, so a difficulty depending on shape non-monotonically — hard at both ends of the weekend axis — would be missed, and the ceiling is a linear ceiling. And shape here is measured once, well before the scored windows: a profile that drifts could matter nearer them, which is one of the audit steps this study skipped.

Across three posts: a foundation model beat a reproduced top-4% feature pipeline by 8.3% of WMAPE with no features, no tuning and no training, and everything afterwards moved the result by a fraction of a percent. The error that remains is not spread evenly — it sits on particular items, durably, and mostly in proportion to how little they sell. What is left after that is the real target, it is about a seventh of the budget, and the first place this study looked for it is now ruled out. Knowing which axis not to spend a month on is worth more than a clustering that would have organised nothing.

item.title: A baseline that earns its place
item.description:
Before comparing a foundation model to anything, there has to be something to compare it to, and a way of comparing that cannot quietly flatter either side. This post builds both: the measuring harness, and a feature-engineered gradient-boosting model reproduced from a public top-4% M5 solution.

The result worth stating up front is how little the 52 engineered features buy over a 28-day mean. That is not a criticism of the solution — it is what makes the comparison in the next post informative.

What a zero means

One target value per series per day: units of one item sold in one Walmart store. History runs 2011-01-29 to 2016-05-22, 1,941 days, 30,490 series. All the work here is on a frozen random sample of 500, drawn once and saved, so every notebook studies the same items.

Show the code 
on_sale = SALES.filter(~pl.col("is_missing"))
per_series = on_sale.group_by("id", "cat_id").agg(
    pl.col("sales").mean().alias("mean_daily"),
    (pl.col("sales") == 0).mean().alias("zero_share"),
)
median_zero = per_series["zero_share"].median()
median_daily = per_series["mean_daily"].median()

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
left.hist(per_series["zero_share"].to_numpy(), bins=np.linspace(0, 1, 21),
          color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, edgecolor="white")
left.set_xlabel("share of on-sale days with zero sales")
left.set_ylabel("number of series")
for category, colour in plots.CATEGORY_COLORS.items():
    values = per_series.filter(pl.col("cat_id") == category)["mean_daily"].to_numpy()
    right.hist(values, bins=np.logspace(-2, 2.5, 28), histtype="step",
               linewidth=2, color=colour, label=category)
right.set_xscale("log")
right.set_xlabel("mean units sold per day (log scale)")
right.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The median series sells 0.55 units a day and is silent on 66% of the days it is on the shelf. Two consequences run through everything that follows.

First, a zero is usually information, not a gap. The one exception is structural: days before an item’s first price in sell_prices.csv, when it was not on the shelf at all. Those are dropped from every history. Everything else is a real zero — the item was available and nobody bought it — and it is part of what the forecast has to get right.

Second, the metric cannot be a percentage error. Dividing by an actual of zero is undefined, and most actuals are zero.

The harness comes first

Two forecast origins, fixed before any model ran:

A (series, window) pair is scored only if it clears three conditions: at least 56 days on sale before the origin, no missing day inside the window, and at least one unit sold in the window. The third is not cosmetic — WMAPE and WQL divide by the window’s total, so a series that sells nothing has no defined error.

What matters more than the conditions is that the count removed by each one is reported separately, and that the surviving list is frozen to disk. A roster that silently changes between models turns every later comparison into a comparison of populations.

Show the code 
md(EVAL_ROSTER.group_by("role").agg(pl.len().alias("scored pairs"),
                                    pl.col("id").n_unique().alias("series")))

Of the 500 sampled series, 473 are scorable on the validation window and 485 on the test window. In both cases every exclusion is the no-sale condition: none of the 500 is short of history, and none has a missing day inside either window.

Five metrics, and what each is for

metric definition what it is for
MAE mean of error in units sold
WMAPE scale-free, survives zeros: the headline
P90 90th percentile of the bad days
WQL mean over of the whole forecast distribution
RQL over-prediction priced at four times under-prediction

is the quantile loss: when the forecast is too low, when it is too high. All sums run over scored (series, day) pairs, never averaged per series and then averaged again.

One identity decides how the next post must be read: for a model that only gives a point forecast, every quantile column is a copy of it, and WQL collapses to WMAPE/100. A probabilistic model can beat that number only by saying something true about its own uncertainty. So WQL is not a fair axis for comparing a point model with a distributional one; MAE, WMAPE and P90 are.

The metric code is checked against three cases whose answers are known in advance: a perfect forecast scores 0 everywhere; a constant zero forecast scores WMAPE 100, WQL 1 and RQL 20; and a point forecast’s WQL equals its WMAPE/100.

Three naive baselines, which are not a formality

Always zero, repeat-last-week, and the mean of the last 28 days. On intermittent data the first is not absurd, and the third is a genuinely strong competitor — which is exactly why it is here.

Show the code 
baselines = ["zero", "seasonal_naive", "moving_average_28d"]
md(rename_models(table_of(baselines, "validation"))
   .select(["model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("WMAPE"))

Note the ordering: repeating last week is barely better than predicting nothing at all, while a flat 28-day mean removes about a fifth of the error. On series this sparse the weekly pattern of a single item is mostly noise, and averaging it away beats reproducing it.

RQL inverts the ranking — the zero forecast wins it outright, 20 against 39. That is the metric doing its job rather than a paradox: RQL prices over-prediction at four times under-prediction, and a forecast of zero can never over-predict.

The features

Rather than invent a feature set, this reproduces one that is public and placed well: btrotta/kaggle-m5 (predict.py), a top-4% M5 solution. Fifty-two features in four families:

  • the series’ own past — lags 1 to 7, means of the last 7/14/28 days, running mean and variance overall and per weekday;
  • the same, two levels up — the item’s department in its store, and the item across all stores, so a thin series borrows the shape of its neighbours;
  • calendar — weekday, month, SNAP benefit days, and an “event uplift” measured as mean sales n days after an event minus the same weekday a week later;
  • price — the current price and its change over 7 and 14 days, plus days since first sale.

The strategy is direct: 28 models, one per forecast day. The model for day k sees sales only up to the origin, with its lag features shifted k days further back, so no forecast is ever fed back as an input and nothing in the window leaks.

Five differences from the original are deliberate, and two of them handicap this reproduction: XGBoost instead of LightGBM with the closest equivalent settings; training on the 500-series sample rather than all 30,490 (the department and item features are still computed on all of them); boosting rounds chosen by early stopping on the last 28 days before the origin, where the original stops on the window it then reports; the event uplift implemented as intended rather than as coded; and missing days defined by the price file.

The second and third of those cost real accuracy. A reproduction that scored better than the original would be the suspicious outcome.

What it buys

Show the code 
models = baselines + ["xgboost_btrotta"]
md(rename_models(pl.concat([
    table_of(models, role).with_columns(pl.lit(role).alias("window"))
    for role in ("validation", "test")
])).select(["window", "model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("window", "WMAPE"))
Show the code 
fig, axes = plots.plot_by_bucket(table_of(models, "validation", by="horizon_bucket"),
                                 metrics.METRICS)
plt.show()

Fifty-two features, 28 trained models and roughly 84 minutes of CPU at the test origin, against a flat mean of the last 28 days: 0.8 WMAPE points on validation, 1.2 on test. The horizon view says where that comes from — the two are nearly tied over the first fortnight, then the mean decays while the model does not, which is the one thing a model with a calendar in it ought to manage.

The per-series view is blunter still.

Show the code 
def per_series_wql(model):
    return metrics.score(scored(model, "validation"), by="id").select(
        "id", pl.col("WQL").alias(f"WQL_{model}"))

volume = (scored("xgboost_btrotta", "validation")
          .group_by("id").agg(pl.col("y").sum().alias("volume")))
comparison = (per_series_wql("moving_average_28d")
              .join(per_series_wql("xgboost_btrotta"), on="id")
              .join(volume, on="id"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
share = plots.index_plot(ax, comparison, "WQL",
                         "moving_average_28d", "xgboost_btrotta", order_by="volume")
plt.show()

XGBoost has the lower WQL on 43% of series. It loses on the majority of items and still wins overall, because the items it wins on are the ones that sell. Pooled metrics weight by volume; a per-series count does not. Both numbers are true, and quoting only the pooled one would be the kind of claim this harness exists to prevent.

What the baseline settles

Three things carry into the next post.

A number to beat. WMAPE 78.8 on validation, 76.4 on test — and the honest framing is that most of that was already available from a 28-day mean.

An axis on which to beat it. XGBoost returns a point forecast, so the comparison is MAE, WMAPE and P90. Its WQL is arithmetic, not a measurement.

A caveat that cuts the other way. XGBoost is trained on squared error, so it estimates a conditional mean. On absolute-error metrics the optimal point forecast is the median, so any model that returns a median starts with a structural advantage on MAE and WMAPE that has nothing to do with forecasting better. Chronos-2 returns a median. That has to be said before the comparison, not after it.

item.title: Chronos-2, knob by knob
item.description:
The previous post left a number to beat: WMAPE 78.8 on the validation window, from 52 hand-built features and 28 trained models. This post hands Chronos-2 the sales history and nothing else.

What the model is

Chronos-2 is a pretrained forecaster of about 120M parameters, a T5-style encoder. It cuts the history into patches of 16 days, embeds each as a vector, and emits the quantiles of the whole horizon in a single forward pass — no token vocabulary, no step-by-step decoding, and the horizon length is an input rather than a trained-in constant. Its point forecast is the median.

M5 was chosen partly because Chronos-2 has no training leakage on it, so a zero-shot number means something here.

Out of the box means: no covariates, no fine-tuning, cross-learning off, default context length. One detail about that default matters more than it looks. The model reads the last context_length days of a series and silently ignores the rest — no warning, no error. On daily M5 data the longest history at the validation origin is 1,885 days, shorter than the documented 2,048 default and far shorter than the 8,192 maximum, so every series is read in full. On a finer-grained grid the same 8,192 steps would be a much shorter span and the default would be quietly truncating most of the history.

Four checks before any number is trusted

Each of these can fail silently, and each would invalidate everything downstream:

  1. Batching is not sharing. With cross-learning off, a series forecast alone and the same series inside a batch of 100 must give the same answer. Largest observed difference: 3·10⁻⁷ units.
  2. The point forecast is the median. The library names the column predictions and computes it in a variable called mean. Largest observed : exactly 0.
  3. The context length changes nothing yet. Forecasting at the 2,048 default must equal forecasting at the model maximum, since no history is that long. Difference: exactly 0.
  4. Quantiles ordered, no missing values. No missing values — but 19.1% of rows have at least one crossing quantile pair. That is the model’s own output, not a bug in the harness, and it is worth knowing before reading any interval as an interval.

Zero-shot

Show the code 
models = ["zero", "seasonal_naive", "moving_average_28d",
          "xgboost_btrotta", "chronos2_vanilla"]
md(rename_models(table_of(models, "validation"))
   .select(["model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("WMAPE"))
Show the code 
fig, axes = plots.plot_by_bucket(table_of(models, "validation", by="horizon_bucket"),
                                 metrics.METRICS)
plt.show()

MAE and WMAPE drop by 10.3% against XGBoost, with no features at all. The engineering that the gradient-boosted baseline needs — lags, rolling windows, per-weekday moments at three aggregation levels — the foundation model extracts from the raw history by reading it.

Two honest deductions from that headline. Part of the 10.3% is the median-versus-mean advantage named at the end of the previous post: XGBoost is trained on squared error and estimates a conditional mean, and on absolute-error metrics the median is the better point forecast regardless of which model is the better forecaster. And P90 goes the other way: Chronos-2 is 3.8% worse than XGBoost on the bad days. On the error you would actually staff for, the feature-engineered model is ahead.

Show the code 
def per_series(model, metric, role="validation"):
    return metrics.score(scored(model, role), by="id").select(
        "id", pl.col(metric).alias(f"{metric}_{model}"))

volume = (scored("chronos2_vanilla", "validation")
          .group_by("id").agg(pl.col("y").sum().alias("volume")))
comparison = (per_series("xgboost_btrotta", "WMAPE")
              .join(per_series("chronos2_vanilla", "WMAPE"), on="id")
              .join(volume, on="id"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
share = plots.index_plot(ax, comparison, "WMAPE",
                         "xgboost_btrotta", "chronos2_vanilla", order_by="volume")
plt.show()

Chronos-2 has the lower WMAPE on 75% of series — unlike the baseline’s win in the previous post, this one is not carried by the high-volume items alone.

Four reasonable ideas that made it worse

Every gain of the gradient-boosted baseline came from handing it information. Chronos-2 accepts extra inputs too, so the obvious next move is to hand it the same knowledge. The question is not rhetorical: anything derived from the timestamp or the target’s own past should be redundant to a model that reads the history, but prices, SNAP days and events are genuinely exogenous and cannot be inferred from sales alone.

Four families were tried, all on the validation window, all against zero-shot:

Show the code 
attempt_files = {
    "calendar": "known_calendar",
    "price": "known_price",
    "SNAP + events": "known_snap_events",
    "all known covariates": "known_all_known",
    "cross-learning": "cross_learning",
    "blanks: past covariate": "blank_past_covariate",
    "blanks: second target": "blank_second_target_both_channels",
    "blanks: NaN-masked": "blank_nan_mask",
}
runs = {"zero-shot": scored("chronos2_vanilla", "validation")}
for label, filename in attempt_files.items():
    table = experiment(filename)
    if "target_name" in table.columns:          # the multivariate run saves both channels
        table = table.filter(pl.col("target_name") == "sales").drop("target_name")
    runs[label] = on_validation(table)

changes = metrics.compare(runs, reference="zero-shot")
widths = pl.DataFrame({
    "model": list(runs),
    "width": [t.select((pl.col("q0.8") - pl.col("q0.2")).mean()).item() for t in runs.values()],
})
reference_width = widths.filter(pl.col("model") == "zero-shot")["width"][0]
widths = widths.with_columns(
    (100 * (pl.col("width") / reference_width - 1)).alias("width_change_%"))

md(changes.join(widths.drop("width"), on="model")
   .filter(pl.col("model") != "zero-shot")
   .select("model", "WMAPE_change_%", "P90_change_%", "WQL_change_%", "width_change_%"))
Show the code 
attempts = changes.filter(pl.col("model") != "zero-shot")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 0.45 * attempts.height + 1.2), sharey=True)
plots.plot_change_bars(axes[0], attempts, "WQL")
plots.plot_change_bars(axes[1], attempts, "WMAPE")
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Read the table block by block.

Known covariates, one block at a time, all lose. Calendar costs 0.36% of WMAPE, price 0.47%, SNAP and events 0.16%. Weekday and month are the clearest case of redundancy — they are recoverable from the timestamps the model already has — but price and SNAP are not, and they lose anyway. Only all four blocks together helps, by 0.54%, which is small enough that a single validation window of 473 series cannot distinguish it from luck.

Cross-learning is the worst single idea tried: +0.85% WMAPE, +1.12% WQL, +3.79% RQL. Letting the series of a batch attend to each other should help a thin series borrow from its neighbours; on this data it hurts. One design note that makes the result about the mechanism rather than about a grouping: the series are sorted by id, so consecutive batches would be nearly single-department, and the order is randomised with a fixed seed before batching.

Every encoding of the long zero runs loses too. About 27% of history days sit inside a run of at least 14 consecutive zero-sale days while the item is on sale. Three ways to point them out: a past-only 0/1 covariate, a second multivariate target, and replacing the values with NaN so the model treats them as unobserved. The first two land at −0.08% WMAPE and +0.10% WQL; masking is the worst result in the study at +2.32% WMAPE and +1.99% WQL.

One trap had to be closed before any of that could be measured: the saved flags were computed on the whole dataset, so a zero run that straddles the origin was partly defined by days the model must not see. Recomputed on history alone, 307 history days change flag.

The diagnostic that inverted

Every run also reports the mean width of its 20–80% band, on the theory that an input the model cannot turn into a rule makes it less sure before it makes it worse. A widening would be the signature of a useless input.

That is not what happened. Seven of the eight attempts came back narrower than zero-shot while scoring worse — cross-learning narrowest of all, at −3.66%. The expected failure mode was hedging; the actual failure mode is confidence that is not earned. Only NaN-masking widened, by 11.3%, and it is also the one whose point forecast degraded most, which is at least self-consistent: told that a quarter of the history is unobserved, the model both loses the information and admits it.

Are the long zero runs predictable at all?

Before building anything on top of a forecast of them — a two-stage model, say — it is worth asking whether they can be forecast. Over the validation window, 2,000 of 13,244 scored (series, day) pairs are inside a real zero run. Two forecasts of them:

source days flagged precision recall
the multivariate is_blank channel, median ≥ 0.5 1,483 0.55 0.41
read off the zero-shot sales forecast 8,696 0.22 0.96

Neither is usable. And the second target has a deeper problem: it is only worth having if a forecast zero run pulls the sales forecast down. Among the 2,106 days where the model is confident of one, its sales forecast is above the zero-shot forecast 38% of the time. The two channels are barely coupled, so the multivariate framing is not merely unhelpful — on more than a third of the days where it fires, it is internally incoherent.

Context length: the one knob that matters, swept 46 ways

The context length is the single setting that decides how much history the model sees. More is not automatically better: a long context can dilute the recent behaviour that drives the next few days, while the far horizon may need more of the past. And because the far horizon and the near horizon may want different answers, the sweep is scored by horizon segment, not overall.

The decision rule was fixed before looking: for days 1–7 and for days 8–28 separately, keep the context with the lowest WQL. If the two differ, stitch — days 1–7 from one, days 8–28 from the other — with the boundary at the edge of the first horizon bucket rather than at a tuned value.

Show the code 
lengths = sorted(
    int(path.name.split("_")[1])
    for path in EXPERIMENTS.glob(f"context_*_{ROSTER}.parquet")
    if path.name.split("_")[1].isdigit() and "origin" not in path.name
)
segment = (pl.when(pl.col("horizon") <= 7).then(pl.lit("days 01-07"))
             .otherwise(pl.lit("days 08-28")).alias("segment"))
sweep = pl.concat([
    metrics.score(on_validation(experiment(f"context_{length}")).with_columns(segment),
                  by="segment").with_columns(pl.lit(length).alias("context_length"))
    for length in lengths
])

longest = max(lengths)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
for name, colour in [("days 01-07", plots.MAIN_COLOR), ("days 08-28", plots.TEXT_COLOR)]:
    part = sweep.filter(pl.col("segment") == name).sort("context_length")
    reference = part.filter(pl.col("context_length") == longest)["WQL"][0]
    ax.plot(part["context_length"].to_numpy(),
            100 * (part["WQL"].to_numpy() / reference - 1),
            color=colour, marker="o", markersize=4, linewidth=1.5, label=name)
ax.axhline(0, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("context length (days, log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("WQL vs whole history (%)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
Show the code 
rows = []
for name in ("days 01-07", "days 08-28"):
    part = sweep.filter(pl.col("segment") == name)
    best = part.sort("WQL").row(0, named=True)
    plateau = part.filter(pl.col("WQL") <= best["WQL"] * 1.01)["context_length"].sort()
    rows.append({"segment": name, "best context": best["context_length"],
                 "WQL": round(best["WQL"], 6),
                 "lengths within 1%": len(plateau),
                 "shortest of those": int(plateau.min())})
md(pl.DataFrame(rows), digits=6)

The shape of that curve is the finding. Below roughly 150 days the model is badly starved and the error rises steeply; above a few hundred the curve is flat to within a fraction of a percent, and the chosen optimum sits on a plateau rather than at a point. Two confirmations that it really is a plateau: more than a dozen lengths fall within 1% of the winner in each segment, and the same selection rule run with WMAPE instead of WQL picks 1,288 for the early segment rather than 1,099 — the same flat region, a different point in it. A CPU run and a GPU run of this sweep disagreed on the coarse-grid winner and still selected the same final pair.

Show the code 
choice = read_json("context_choice")
early, late = choice["early_context"], choice["late_context"]
from m5_chronos2.chronos2 import stitch

candidates = {
    "whole history": experiment(f"context_{longest}"),
    f"best single length ({late})": experiment(f"context_{late}"),
    f"stitch {early} -> {late}": stitch(experiment(f"context_{early}"),
                                        experiment(f"context_{late}"),
                                        choice["early_last_day"]),
}
md(metrics.compare({k: on_validation(v) for k, v in candidates.items()},
                   reference="whole history")
   .select(["model"] + [f"{m}_change_%" for m in metrics.METRICS]), digits=3)

So: a 46-length sweep, a selection rule fixed in advance, a stitch across two regimes — and the whole exercise removes 0.11% of WMAPE and 0.08% of WQL. Reading the entire history, which is what the model does if you tell it nothing, is within a tenth of a percent of the best configuration available.

LoRA, aimed at the long horizon

Full fine-tuning would update 120M weights. LoRA freezes them and learns a rank-8 correction to the attention matrices and the output layer — a few hundred thousand trainable parameters, which is what makes the run affordable at all. Rank 8, learning rate 1e-5, 1,000 steps, effective batch 32.

The protocol keeps the fine-tune away from what it is scored on: training windows are cut at random from history up to origin − 28 days, the 28 days immediately before the origin are the validation target scored every 100 steps, the best checkpoint by that loss is kept, and the forecast window is never touched. The test-origin model is a fresh fine-tune with the same configuration on the longer history, exactly as the baseline was retrained per window.

Since nothing forces a model to forecast at the context length it was tuned at, all four pairings were tried.

Show the code 
def lora(finetune_context, predict_context, origin):
    name = (f"lora_ctx{finetune_context}_steps1000_lr1e-05_bs32"
            f"_context_{predict_context}_origin{origin}")
    return experiment(name)

configs = {f"zero-shot, context {c}": experiment(f"context_{c}") for c in (early, late)}
for finetune_context in (late, early):
    for predict_context in (early, late):
        configs[f"LoRA@{finetune_context}, context {predict_context}"] = lora(
            finetune_context, predict_context, VALIDATION_ORIGIN)

by_segment = metrics.compare(
    {name: on_validation(table).with_columns(segment) for name, table in configs.items()},
    by="segment")
md(by_segment.select("model", "segment", "WQL").pivot(on="segment", index="model",
                                                      values="WQL"), digits=6)

Per-segment winners: fine-tuned at 1,099 and forecasting at 1,099 for days 1–7, fine-tuned at 1,099 and forecasting at 1,829 for days 8–28. The long segment is a cross pairing — tuned at one length, predicting at another — which training and predicting at a single length would never have surfaced. It is also the kind of result that is easy to over-read: the gap between it and the next configuration is in the fourth decimal of WQL.

The cost is worth recording. On the laptop CPU this measured 21.7 s per training step and 126 s per evaluation pass: 6.4 hours per fine-tune, up to 25.5 hours for the plan. The same work on a GTX 1080 took about 32 minutes per run. Every number in this section that is compared with another was produced on the same device, because CPU and GPU disagree in the third decimal of WQL — enough to invert a ranking this tight.

The one measurement on the test window

The test window was used for no decision anywhere in this post.

Show the code 
final = ["zero", "seasonal_naive", "moving_average_28d", "xgboost_btrotta",
         "chronos2_vanilla", "chronos2_best"]
md(rename_models(table_of(final, "test"))
   .select(["model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("WMAPE"))
Show the code 
fig, axes = plots.plot_by_bucket(table_of(final, "test", by="horizon_bucket"),
                                 metrics.METRICS)
plt.show()

The zero-shot model and the final model are the same model to within a rounding error. On MAE, WMAPE and P90 the tuned model is marginally worse; on WQL it is 0.23% better. Set against XGBoost, zero-shot gains 8.32% of WMAPE and the final model 8.29% — the tuning removed a sliver rather than adding one.

Show the code 
volume_test = (scored("chronos2_best", "test")
               .group_by("id").agg(pl.col("y").sum().alias("volume")).sort("volume"))
examples = [volume_test["id"][int(q * (volume_test.height - 1))]
            for q in (0.98, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25)]
loaded = {m: pl.read_parquet(ARTIFACTS / "predictions" / f"{m}_{ROSTER}.parquet")
             .filter(pl.col("origin") == TEST_ORIGIN)
          for m in ("xgboost_btrotta", "chronos2_vanilla", "chronos2_best")}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(examples), 1, figsize=(11, 10), sharex=True)
for ax, series_id in zip(axes, examples):
    one = TRUTH.filter(pl.col("id") == series_id)
    past = one.filter(pl.col("date") <= TEST_ORIGIN,
                      pl.col("date") > TEST_ORIGIN - timedelta(days=84))
    actual = one.filter(pl.col("date") > TEST_ORIGIN,
                        pl.col("date") <= TEST_ORIGIN + timedelta(days=28))
    pick = lambda m: loaded[m].filter(pl.col("id") == series_id)
    plots.plot_fan(ax, past, pick("chronos2_best"), actual,
                   color=plots.MODEL_COLORS["chronos2_best"], label="Chronos-2 final")
    for model, name in [("chronos2_vanilla", "Chronos-2 zero-shot"),
                        ("xgboost_btrotta", "XGBoost")]:
        rows = pick(model)
        ax.plot(rows["date"].to_numpy(), rows["y_pred"].to_numpy(),
                color=plots.MODEL_COLORS[model], linewidth=1.2, label=name)
    ax.axvline(TEST_ORIGIN, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=0.8, linestyle=":")
    ax.set_title(series_id, loc="left")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1))
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What this adds up to

Out of the box, on data it had never seen, Chronos-2 beat a reproduced top-4% feature pipeline by 8.3% of WMAPE. Then: four families of extra information, a 46-length sweep of its most important setting, a stitch across horizon segments and a LoRA fine-tune — and the combined effect of all of it is a fraction of a percent, in the wrong direction on the point forecast.

The flat part of that story is not a failure of effort; it is a measurement. Every configuration tried lands in the same narrow band, which is what a ceiling looks like from the inside. The honest next question is not “which knob was missed” but “is this a limit of the tuning, or of the problem?” — and that is answerable, which is what the third post does.

One lever is left untried here, and it is the one worth testing properly: treat different series differently — fine-tune per group, cross-learn inside a group, one model per group. That has a precondition which can be tested before any of it is built.
